newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israelis turn to Bible after helicopters crash.
newsitem.headline: Israelis turn to Bible after helicopters crash.

text.p: A divine sign or just an eerie coincidence?

That's the question many Israelis were asking after discovering that the weekly biblical passage read in synagogues last Saturday contained the name of the village over which two army helicopters collided three days later, killing 73 soldiers.
Newspapers on Thursday highlighted the reference to Shaar Yishuv -- the name of the prophet Isaiah's son and the modern-day northern Israeli farming community.
The mass-circulation Yedioth Ahronoth daily said many people had telephoned the newspaper to point out "clues to the tragedy" in Isaiah 7:3.
"Then said the Lord unto Isaiah, Go forth now to meet Ahaz, thou, and Shaar Yishuv thy son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool in the highway of the fuller's field," the passage says.

The chapter describes the attempt by Syria and the northern kingdom of Israel to coerce the southern kingdom of Judea into joining their campaign against Assyria. Isaiah and Shaar Yishuv urged Judea's King Ahaz not to enter into a foreign alliance.

It goes on to mention "two tails of these smoking firebrands" -- a reference to the kings of Israel and Syria -- but which Yedioth said some of the callers took to mean the two tails of the helicopters that crashed in flames.
The scriptures have been cited in another recent milestone in Israeli history: the November 1995 assassination of Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin.
Rabin was killed in the week in which the biblical story of Abraham's near-sacrifice of his son Isaac (Yitzhak in Hebrew) was read in synagogues.
